segments.speaker: Abbye Feeley
segments.text: Good morning, council. Abbye Feeley, administrator for development and economic opportunity. This morning, we're here to talk about the fee study, to workshop the fee study that was completed by raftelis. With us this morning is joe Williams from raftelis, tristen townsend from raftelis, as well as JC Hudgison, our Building Official and -- Chief Building Official and construction services manager. I need a little bit more coffee. Eric Cotton, Development Coordination manager, Dennis Fernandez, our historic preservation manager, and Brandon Campbell, our director of mobility. Since the fee study included all of those areas. I'm going to turn over to joe. Joe is really going to present to you on the study what we did, how we did it, what it showed us. And we do have a recommended fee schedule. As I mentioned to you in previous updates, that schedule includes what we call kind of level setting and practicality of some of those fees. These fees are only recommendations before you today. We're here to start a dialogue, to have a conversation, to talk about what those fees are. Like I said, how they were determined, where we're going with this, what implementation of this would look like over a number of years. In addition to that, we will be having a public meeting on October 21st at hanna city center. We have set up a website on the fee study that has the document out there. We've also set out some correspondence to our advisory groups that our teams meet with on a regular basis as well as all of our accela users in anticipation of sharing this information. We also have Dana Crosby with us today from the city attorney's office if there are any questions in relation to how this relates to senate bill 180 and us increasing the fees. The way we are looking at this is for a March 1st effective date, which would go in with the water and wastewater fee increases that you all have already approved, and it is a multiyear. And I'll let joe go into that a little bit, but for construction services, it's over five years, and for Development Coordination, historic preservation it would be three years. We also have some comparison for you today of how we are in relation to other cities, what's going on, and we'll go from there. I'll turn it over to joe. What we'd like to do is work through the entire presentation and then we are going to work as a team to answer any questions that you may have.

segments.text: Good morning, joe. Start with your name, please. Joe Williams from raftelis. Thank you for having us. segments.text: We got it. Good to go. There is a good amount of information, but leave some room for questions, not go --

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Hey, this is your show. That's the idea we have. We definitely want to answer good questions. So, when we first got engaged, we really were focused on the building fees, construction services division, and then talking through with Abbye and others. There was a desire also to look at Development Coordination, the architectural review boards, the city clerk fees for petitions related to a lot of these fees that we would be updating and the mobility right-of-way. There's some administrative related fees in their department that hadn't been updated in many years either. Talk about a lot of these fees even date back to the early 2000s. 2000, 2006 in some cases, construction services was a little bit more recent, but they are still pushing a good eight years or so since really being updated. How did we get here? Construction services, again, back in 2021, they did a major upgrade to their billing software, their permit software. Again, we'll talk a little bit about their existing fee structure. Won't dwell on it too much, but there's thousands of individual rates on their various schedules. Once that was created in the new software, it was really hard to update and manage over time, so we have gone through a major simplification effort, try to make it so it can be updated more efficiently each year going forward. We understand that there's various policy direction over time, again, covid was a huge factor and a lot of this on keeping fees level, not looking at specific increases during a challenging time. That has contributed and changing legislative landscape. The Florida statutes sections related to especially the building fees has been updated tremendously the past five or six years. It's created a lot of additional regulation, timelines, things on JC's department that have required increase in staffing, increases in other costs to administer a similar level of effort and to meet all those requirements. He's had that issue and then the permit activity again, spiked early in the covid years and then it started to normalize again now. Also hurricane activity. There is a natural ebb and flow in the permit activity and sort of on a slight, slight reduction in that area right now. That leads directly to permit revenues. So our approach, again, study approach, we want to look at what is the full cost of administering these departments. When someone comes in for a specific type of permit, what is all the staff effort and necessary overhead costs of operating a department that go into providing these efforts. So that's what we've identified in the study. We've worked with staff on an initial phasing plan. We'll talk about certain fees where we calculated the cost that staff felt was relatively high, and the recommended plan, some of those have been set below the actual costs that we've calculated. Again, there are several factors that go into that. Do have some latitude within your fee setting to set fees below the actual costs. Again, we met in detail on every work flow, every fee with staff on understanding what goes into each one of these things, who is involved, how much time are people spending on average cases, and that's how we've developed the fee study. So, construction services, really what I'll hit on here, this is the building department administering if there's new construction, changes on properties for accessory structures, additions of pools, major construction type things, electrical, plumbing, and this is pretty strictly governed by Florida statutes, especially on the revenue expense side at this point. It's about 100 employees and $22 million annual budget right now. On the left side, you'll see a small, relatively small snapshot of the existing fee schedule.

segments.speaker: Alan Clendenin
segments.text: Printed by our CFO. We don't want to you try to read all the fees. Again, this is, if you opened up one of the schedules on the city's website, there's probably seven different files that each have five to ten pages of fees that look just like this. It's all tied back to the international business code, construction types, occupancy types and huge range of fees. Again, very hard to administer and update. It took a lot of work and a lot of massaging of the data to get it to where we felt comfortable recommending a new fee structure, but that's what we have on the slide here, residential grouping and commercial grouping. The fees we're showing you are for new construction. There are some discounted rates with a very similar structure for other types of phased buildings or shell buildings or tenant improvements, things that are related, but relatively lower effort for the building department based on all the plan reviews and inspections that go into things. Simplification of the fee structure. Revenue enhancement, I'll touch on this one a little bit. Basically, what's happened is over the past several years, again, with all the additional regulations that have been introduced, the department has grown. So there's been a growing staff to meet all the timelines, the regulations, all those things that go into it. Revenues have stayed about stable, even slight decreases the past few years. Again, this is a department where if nobody pulled a permit, there would be zero dollars coming in. On the utility side, you at least have base charges. People need to use water. It's consistent revenue. Here, they can go from zero to, you know, 20 million in any given year. Now, you're typically operating in the 14 to $16 million range the past several years. As we showed you, JC has a budget of 22 million for this upcoming year. It's been at that level for the past few years or so. So we needed revenue enhancement. When we simplified the fee structure, we made it so that when we set those rates, there was additional revenue that was going to be generated, and then that sort of strung through the process. Then we have each of the individual permit fees which are more fixed fees for services, if you come for a mechanical permit or plumbing permit, simple plumbing, there is a fixed fee for it. Those fees are increasing as well. That's going to generate additional revenue. There's resubmittals, additional plan review fees, things like that. So we're getting additional revenue from a few different areas. So this is -- a couple of different things, there is the enhancement fund and there's the primary operating fund that JC has. This is really a picture of the primary operations fund. You can see it is less than 22 million. The enhancement fund is an additional surcharge added on to the building permit that covers a lot of the technology vehicle related cost of the department. So this is really just the operating fund. And you can see that in 2026, the revenues, which are the line, the green line, are pretty well below the expenses for the department. Again, it's been like that for a couple, few years now, but what we have to say is during covid and kind of that time when activity was higher and before a lot of the new regulations came, the division was operating at a surplus, had accumulated a fairly strong cash reserve position, and the past few years really spent it down. We show that you on the next slide. It's been spent down. We're at the point where the '27 budget, if there were no rate adjustments, is showing we probably would be relying on the General Fund to support the department. So now we have these rate adjustments identified. We're hoping to not be in that situation beginning in 2027. So that's the slide. You can see down below, $5 million in a cash reserve position for a $20 million department. Florida statutes allows you to have a reserve balance up to the average of the prior four years of budgeted expenditures for that department. Again, we could have a balance closer to 15 to 16 million per statutes, but we've spent it down, kept fees low or level over the past several years. So we're kind of just at that point where we need to start moving back in the other direction to be a fully sustaining, special revenue fund. That's one specifically set for the special revenue fund, supposed to operate like a business. Supposed to generate the revenues to cover the cost of operations. That is the general intent. Small list of example fees, again, this is demonstrated to show you there is a wide range of different impacts. In the full report, there are exhibits. There are longer fee tables showing you all the different fees. We want to just show a few examples here. Not going to go into great detail, but there is a range. It's not all 15%. Sometimes it's 30%. Sometimes in rare cases there's some small decreases. Again, that goes into some of the discussions with staff on trying to keep reasonable fees in certain areas, consistency for different types of things. Just a high level example, again, we worked with the departments, detailed reviews, detailed work flows, and this accessory structure will serve two purposes. We summarized it to a pretty high level. Intake and processing. This includes correspondence with applicants along the way. Plan review, inspection time, and then some vehicle usage time. And there are other overhead factors kind of built into there. So this one, we calculated a fee of $480 working with staff. This is one of the fees where it is very homeowner application based where they are going to be getting a shed or another small structure on their property. If we are setting the fee too high, there's some level of concern that people will stop coming for permits. Then it's going to be a more costly effort to pursue after-the-fact permits, trying to get them to pay, comply. It's much better for the department and the city overall to have the permits come up front as they are supposed to, more efficient, better process, so that is considered in not going to the full fee in the situation. And there are a few other fees like that along the way, residential and commercial. So that's kind of a first pass. These are initial recommendations. We're all here looking for feedback and then the community meetings to get additional feedback as well. We have some comparisons. Really the highlight here, you'll see that we are going to be increasing fees for different types of construction activity, but we don't feel like we're going outside of a lot of our neighbors or other areas in the state. A lot of these communities that are on the comparison do have a fee structure that may or may not be in alignment with the most recent Florida house bill 803 updates. They likely will be pursuing updates to their fee schedules as well or may actively be. So we'll say that. There is a lot of changing legislation where building fees are being updated all throughout the state right now. Just a few more examples. If there are any questions on these, we can come back to them.

segments.text: The thing that concerns me about this is that as the building gets larger, the rate gets smaller. I really don't want to be incentivizing larger residential properties. Commercial, that's fine. But residential, what we're trying to do is build more housing here. Some of that is going to be smaller by nature. Anything that's above 5,000 square feet, they really need to be paying that 33.35. I'm sorry. If you are building a massive home, then you can afford massive, like, fees. I don't have any sympathy for that. If you are in tier one and tier two, those are the places that I want to bring down. That's what we need to incentivize. We need to incentivize smaller homes. For me, I might flip that whole thing. I don't know how we would do that, but really, we want to incentivize more smaller houses. Also, the other thing that comes to mind is affordable housing set-asides. As we're looking at these fee increases, we also really want to look at people who are building affordable housing. By affordable housing, I mean owner occupied. If they are owner occupied, I really believe we need to reduce or eliminate funding or fees for affordable housing that people are going to owner occupy. Now, there still might be a reduction or something for apartment buildings, but really -- and by AMI. If we can't reduce them wholly, something by AMI. But again, I'm talking about ownership for residential. I don't really know -- I mean, I know we probably need to do something for commercial, but home ownership residential, I just had a really good conversation with habitat, and they are looking at ways to build more housing, and this is one of the things they said could tremendously help them. A reduction in impact fees. Because all they do is build owner occupied, and that to me is very important. Thank you. Otherwise, this is very interesting. Also, you skipped through quite a few, like, you were just showing us, if you could go to the last one of the variations of between different cities, this one -- no, one more. Then go back. Go back one more. This concerns me. Our proposed are going to be lower than Hillsborough county already is. And I know that -- but I understand -- so my guess is what we're trying to do is incentivize people building this stuff within the city. Is that the reason that we're sticking kind of lower here?

segments.text: There is a relationship between setting the tiers and the cost recovery. As buildings scale, it doesn't always -- the effort from the department doesn't always scale quite as fast.

Is that one of the reasons that we're -- and whoever has their phone that is making those jingles, if you could turn that to mute, that would be great.

segments.text: Abbye Feeley. When we looked at that with joe and the team, I don't know at this point in the study it was really about cost recovery. What is it taking us to do the work? I'm tracking, because on affordable housing also, like we offer right now expedited permitting. We offer no connection fee. I always get capacity fee and connection fee messed up. But for water and wastewater. We have other things. We have not by statute been able to waive impact fees.

But how are they coming up with those numbers? Just because they are our neighbor.

segments.speaker: Abbye Feeley

segments.speaker: Lynn Hurtak

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: First point of order, Mr. Chair. Especially on workshop days, could you please -- nobody has done this yet, could you please enforce the rule that we have to be called on to speak and we don't interrupt each other. Because we're going to have probably more back and forth later. But I want to make sure we do it in an organized way. Just like we can't hear, the public can't hear if we're talking over each other. Just for the public, this is the fees we're paying, not impact fees, right? We're not talking about impact fees.

segments.speaker: Abbye Feeley
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: This is just application. Okay. Just to clarify that. The law says you can have -- you said just to repeat what you said, you can have a certain fund on top of it, a reserve fund on top, but we can't charge -- is there a certain percentage, besides reserve fund, a percentage mark-up that we can charge on top of what the actual cost is. Or we charge the actual cost plus whatever the reserve fund is. You have the ability, if you have cushion from where your current reserve is to where your reserve can be justified, you can set the fees a little higher to fund a reserve and fund future capital replacement needs.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Ms. Feeley Mentioned an expedited fee. Is that in here? Did I miss That? Could you talk to us about those fees? I forgot what you called a rushed fee or expedited fee, additional fee.

segments.speaker: Abbye Feeley
segments.text: Abbye Feeley. The legislation from the state requires if you're using private provider that reviews have to be done within ten days. When the private provider submits that, it has to be done within ten days. If it's not within ten days, you start paying back the fee to the applicant at certain percentages for the amount of time it takes longer. Going back to the ftes and how our ftes have increased, part of that is because the state mandates to complete reviews within certain times because we don't want to return fee. We want to keep the department stable.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: I know your office gets a lot of complaints because there's so much growth in the area. You've come before us so many times to talk about how you're trying to address that. Right now we're talking about cost recovery with the process you have, and there's a lot of money there. Is there a higher level of service that we could offer if customers have to trade off between speed and cost? So set aside the outside services, is there a way that if somebody needs to do something urgently that they could pay more? Is there an expedited team you could put on that we could charge an extra fee for? Or extra people you could hire that we could do cost recovery on so we could provide these faster. My question to you is, if we provided more resources to provide a better service or faster service, would that help you? And then how would we cost recover that?

segments.speaker: Abbye Feeley
segments.text: So, right now, as joe mentioned, sometimes the permitting ebbs and flows, right? We do keep two teams on contract and we have gone to using one of those teams for our tenant improvements. If you are coming in to get a tenant improvement, you went across the street to the suntrust, you'll put your office in there now, those, we use an outside team to do those now. Those reviews get done in three days for the building part. They still require life safety review, which is the fire element of this, which life safety does get reviewed as part of the permit process, but they are part of Tampa Fire Rescue and fire marshals office.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Are we recovering any of that cost in here?

segments.speaker: Joe Williams
segments.text: We do have fire in certain -- commercial --

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: The budget for fire has been under what it should have been for years. If there is a way to do cost recovery where we could help expedite that. I pass on the complaints to Ms. Feeley, and she always does a great job with her staff of responding to them. A bunch of them are around the fire review. If we could make sure that the team and fire is covered by these costs --

segments.speaker: JC Hudgison
segments.text: JC Hudgison, Chief Building Official. There are two pieces to your question there. For the expedite, yes. It's in the system to be double the fee to do it in half the time. However, the concern that was just brought up, because we are the one-stop shop, I can expedite the building side but the other pieces, whether it's fire or other pieces, stormwater, Solid Waste. So now it gets a little tricky because we could finish our part but don't technically give you the full review. We don't necessarily promote it as much as we should. There are options. We have a large scale project team that deals with larger projects as we go through. We also had tiered permits. We didn't get into that too much. The building permit, all inclusive, everybody looks at everything. Tier below, your miscellaneous permits. So those don't take as long and we have a project process for that. And then trade permits. Somebody coming in to get a hot water heater, we've expedited those as fast as we can. Those are instant issuance. As soon as the contractor comes in, licensed contractor, wants to replace a water heater at somebody's home, as long as a licensed contractor and pays the fee, issued. At that point it is on the inspection. Some of the things we already sped up about as fast as we can and practical as we can to still make sure we get the reviews.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: The thing I would encourage you all to do in working with the consultants, my colleague pointed out that our costs are lower than the county and other cities, what you have on this chart here, it could be that we're just more efficient and that we don't spend as much. But the other thing is that if there are expedited services or ways to improve customer service, I would ask you all -- I know you do this already -- ask you all to take another look at it just to see because real estate is so much of a big part of our economic engine in our area, how can we move some of these faster. I would like to get every day ten compliments on how awesome they think you guys are. When you fix the problem, they think you are awesome. It's an issue that's been with the development community forever. If we could solve that, by raising the rates by 20 cents and have a team that gets these done faster, that would really make a lot of people in the community happy. segments.text: Michael Perry, deputy chief financial officer. Once the construction services fund goes negative balance, probably have to come from the General Fund.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson

segments.speaker: Michael Perry
segments.text: I'm sorry, sir.

segments.speaker: Bill Carlson
segments.text: Who pays the General Fund?

Anyway, thank you.

segments.text: We've had it.

segments.text: That is correct. The other thing I wanted to add to that, we've even decreased that cost because we've now gone to virtual inspection. segments.text: One more question. So then in logic what we're doing here is creating something like, we have a water, wastewater, Solid Waste, and parking. You're producing your money to carry --
